newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: FEATURE - Moslem Mauritania to stop child brides.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Moslem Mauritania to stop child brides.

text.p: Moslem Mauritania, keen to erase a lingering perception abroad that it is out of tune with modern realities, is planning to outlaw the practice of child brides.
At the same time, the former French colony at the crossroads between the Arab world and black Africa is working hard to increase the number of girls in primary school and higher education.
The reforms are part of a drive to liberalise the West Africa nation's economy and encourage foreign investment.
Opposition and women's rights activists, some of whom dismiss the reforms as window dressing to impress Western donors or investors, acknowledge a change for the better.
But they say that true change, in which women enjoy real equality of opportunity with men, remains a distant hope.

"Mauritania, which applies sharia law, is currently drafting a Family Code," Sinnya Mint Sidi Haiba, Secretary of State for Women's Affairs, told Reuters in an interview, adding that the aim was to make 18 the minimum legal age for marriage.
"In isolated villages you can find early marriage with brides as young as 10 or 11 but in towns the average is 18."

Sidi Haiba said the technical phase of drafting the Family Code had been completed. The aim, she added, was to tighten up legal safeguards governing such matters as marriage, divorce and the duties of separated fathers to pay for their children.
"The problem is one of proper administrative measures."

This month's legislative election, the second since the advent of multi-party politics in 1991, gave Mauritania its first woman national assembly member. The deputy, Lalla Zeina Mint Sbaghou, member of the ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party, is also a Harratin, a descendant of the slaves held by Mauritania's dominant Arab-speaking Moors.

Sidi Haiba said the practice of child brides denied girls a proper education in a country which was keen to expand the role in society of women, who already enjoy the right to equal pay and, in theory, equal opportunity.
"The girls marry early, have children very early and that cuts their studies," she said.
Sidi Haiba said 65 to 67 percent of all girl now received a primary school education compared to 77 to 80 percent of boys.

World Bank representative Claude Delapierre puts an alternative spin on the benefits of sending girls to school -- it can also be a way of curbing the population in a country where modern birth control methods may not be readily accepted.
"If you send the girls to school, they marry later, they go on to work and they have fewer children," he said.
Mauritania has a population growth rate of about 2.9 percent, lower than many neighbours in the region.

This has a positive impact on growth figures. With its gross domestic product growing by 4.5 percent in 1995, Mauritania enjoyed real growth of 1.6 percent -- above the World Bank's global target of one percent.

Sidi Haiba said President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya, who seized power in 1984 and won a six-year term in 1992 elections, was keen to ensure women played a much greater role in the economic life of the nation of 2.2 million people. "He has said that women should play the same role as their brothers."
Sidi Haiba said the government was trying to persuade families in rural areas to send their girls to primary school. Schools are free in Mauritania.
She said women were starting to make their mark in such sectors as education, health and in business. "We have noticed that (Mauritanian) women are gifted at business management."
Women in professions such as law and medicine remain few. Out of more than 200 barristers only five are women and there are only about 10 women doctors, but that is changing.
"There are many young women studying medicine abroad. In France, in Syria or in Russia," Sidi Haiba said.

The government is helping women organise themselves in cooperatives -- of which there are 2,000. One group has raised 500 million ouguiya ($3.6 million) -- half from savings and half from loans -- to build a shopping centre near the presidency.
"In the past, banks were wary of women. Access to credit was difficult...but now they are starting to show confidence in women," Sidi Haiba said.
Sidi Haiba said that in the eyes of the law there was no distinction between men and women. "They have the same rights and the same responsibilities."
Critics of the government, while they acknowledge changes for the better, say that true equality will remain a dream until there is a change of mentality among Mauritania's men.

"It's not a question of studies, it's the work she does and the responsibility she is given," one professional woman commented. "Even if you grant her the right to study, everything will be done to stop her getting beyond that level."

Sidi Haiba, asked whether Mauritania could one day have a woman president, said that women had the right to stand but acknowledged that it was not likely to happen soon. "It's a question of mentality. It could take time," she said.
($1=138 ouguiya)
